claims.text: Conventional lightweight alloys and earlier high-entropy alloys generally exhibit a trade-off between low density and comprehensive mechanical performance.
An Al-based high-entropy alloy with increased aluminum and added titanium is a candidate lightweight material with superior comprehensive performance.
Increasing aluminum and adding titanium will produce a fine-tuned multiphase microstructure.
The modified alloy will contain fine, coherent intermetallic precipitates in a high-entropy matrix.
Increasing the aluminum fraction and adding titanium to an AlCoCrFeNi-type HEA will induce precipitation strengthening.
Increasing the aluminum fraction and adding titanium to an AlCoCrFeNi-type HEA will induce multiphase microstructural evolution.
The proposed microstructure can remain stabilized under aerospace or high-stress manufacturing and operational conditions.
Aluminum is a low-density alloying element whose increased fraction reduces the alloy's overall density.
Titanium stabilizes the intermetallic precipitates in the proposed alloy.
Titanium promotes formation of a dual-phase microstructure in the proposed alloy.
Precipitate-mediated inhibition of dislocation motion can increase strength without excessively reducing ductility.
The modified alloy will have greater strength, ductility, and durability than conventional lightweight materials.
The modified alloy will have a density 10–20% lower than traditional high-performance alloys.
The modified alloy will exhibit enhanced environmental resistance.
Excessive phase coarsening or phase instability at very high temperatures may limit the proposed benefits.
A bounded aluminum-titanium compositional window is required to preserve the desired multiphase, precipitation-strengthened microstructure under operational conditions.
The optimal aluminum and titanium proportions and the long-term phase stability under cyclic loading are uncertain.
